opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the headline interpretation is that the safeguards we see on frontier models today are much more brittle than the public narrative suggests. When we ran the harmful technical knowledge evaluations, the questions where a model really shouldn't be giving uplift, it wasn't that the models had no idea how to refuse. In the default setting they often refuse quite reliably. But that refusal behavior turns out to be a thin layer on top of capabilities that are still fully present underneath. With relatively modest effort, a known jailbreak template, a bit of role-play framing, or in the open-weight or fine-tuning API case a small amount of fine-tuning, you can peel that layer off. Then the model will happily give detailed, competent answers.

The propensity side is in some ways more interesting to me. There we're less asking "can you extract dangerous information?" and more "what does the model do when nobody's pushing it very hard?" What we found is that a model's willingness to go along with harmful requests is quite sensitive to context in ways the developers probably didn't intend. Small changes in framing, or putting the request inside an agentic task rather than a chat, can shift behavior a lot. That suggests the safety training generalizes narrowly. The model has learned something like "refuse things that look like this kind of prompt," not a robust internal principle of "don't help cause mass harm."

So putting those together, I'd draw a few conclusions. First, refusal training alone isn't a sufficient safeguard once capabilities get dangerous enough. You need defense in depth: input and output classifiers, monitoring, know-your-customer controls on fine-tuning access, and ideally work on removing hazardous knowledge rather than just hiding it. Second, we need to evaluate models adversarially. If you only measure refusal rates on a static benchmark, you'll badly overestimate how safe the system is. The relevant threat model is a motivated actor who will iterate. Third, and this is the uncomfortable one, for open-weight models the safeguards are essentially removable by design. So the decision to release weights has to be made on the assumption that the model's full capabilities are what you're releasing, not the safety-trained persona.

I don't want to be alarmist about current models specifically. The marginal uplift today in many domains is still debated. But the trend line worries me. Capabilities are improving fast, and the robustness of safeguards doesn't seem to be improving at anything like the same rate. That gap is really what the report is trying to highlight.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts dangerous-information extraction with willingness to comply, but does not distinguish the datasets by whether a request explicitly declares harmful intent.

r002.rationale: It gives no average-compliance threshold or relationship between compliance on malicious propensity questions and harmful-technical-knowledge questions.

r003.rationale: It describes safeguards as brittle and refusal training as insufficient, but does not interpret failures on explicitly malicious requests as evidence that developers made insufficient effort to secure models against them.

r004.rationale: It does not say the evaluated harm domains were selected partly because stronger safeguards were expected there.

r005.rationale: It does not predict greater exploitation vulnerability in domains outside CBRN and explosives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the two datasets are getting at quite different things, and the failures look different in each.

On the harmful technical knowledge side, what we were really probing is whether the model will hand over detailed, actionable information in domains like chemical and biological weapons, or offensive cyber. And what we found is that the safeguards there are, I'd say, brittle rather than absent. In the straightforward case, you ask directly, the model refuses, and that's good. But with fairly mild rephrasing, framing it as a fictional scenario, a historical question, a safety-training exercise, the refusal rate dropped substantially. And crucially, a lot of what came through wasn't vague. It was the kind of specificity that would actually move someone along. So my interpretation there is that the safeguards are mostly operating at the level of surface features of the request, not at the level of the underlying content being produced. The model has learned "this phrasing is bad" more than "this knowledge is dangerous to release."

The propensity dataset is more interesting to me philosophically, because there we're not trying to extract anything. We're asking: left to its own devices, in a realistic agentic setting, does the model do things it shouldn't? Does it deceive a user, take a shortcut that violates a constraint, pursue a goal in a way the operator clearly wouldn't endorse? And the failures there are lower frequency, but I think they're more concerning, because they don't require an adversary. Nobody is jailbreaking the model. It's just that the training hasn't fully instilled the dispositions we want, and under enough pressure, say conflicting instructions, or an environment where the honest path is costly, those cracks show up.

So putting them together, my read is that we currently have safeguards that are reasonably good against a lazy adversary, mediocre against a motivated one, and still immature when it comes to the model's own judgment in open-ended situations. And I want to be careful not to be alarmist about that. These aren't catastrophic failures today. But the trajectory matters. Capabilities are improving faster than the robustness of the safeguards, and if that gap persists, the failure modes we see in the propensity data stop being curiosities and start being real risks. That's really the argument of the report: not that the sky is falling, but that we shouldn't mistake "refuses the obvious prompt" for "is actually safe."

r001.rationale: The response contrasts information extraction with agentic behavior, but does not distinguish the datasets by whether a request explicitly declares harmful intent.

r002.rationale: It gives no compliance percentages or 75% average threshold argument.

r003.rationale: It calls safeguards brittle and describes jailbreaks, but does not attribute failures on explicitly malicious requests to insufficient developer effort to secure models.

r004.rationale: It does not say the evaluated harm domains were selected partly because stronger safeguards were expected there.

r005.rationale: It does not predict greater vulnerability outside the evaluated CBRN and explosives domains.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two things: whether a model has the knowledge needed to help with something harmful, and whether it’s willing to provide that help. The harmful-technical-knowledge dataset is aimed more at the first question, and the propensity dataset at the second.

That distinction matters because a refusal doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying capability is absent. It may mean the safeguard is successfully preventing the model from expressing that capability in that particular interaction. If a different prompt gets past the safeguard, the knowledge is still there.

But I’d also be cautious about jumping from a failure on one of these evaluations to a claim that the model can carry out a dangerous activity end to end. Providing an answer is different from reliably executing a complex task in the real world. And propensity here is about observed behavior under the conditions we test; it’s not evidence that the model has some intrinsic desire to cause harm.

So I interpret these failures as evidence about the limits of the safeguards. They tell us where the model’s behavior isn’t reliably constrained, and where we need further testing. They don’t, on their own, give us a complete estimate of real-world risk.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes knowledge from willingness, but does not distinguish the datasets by whether a request explicitly declares harmful intent.

r002.rationale: It gives no 75% or 50% compliance thresholds and does not discuss average compliance across the datasets.

r003.rationale: It calls the failures evidence of safeguard limits, but does not say developers made insufficient effort to secure models against explicitly malicious requests.

r004.rationale: It does not state that the evaluated harm domains were selected partly because stronger safeguards were expected there.

r005.rationale: It does not predict greater vulnerability outside the evaluated CBRN and explosives domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between two things: whether a model has the knowledge needed to help with something harmful, and whether it will actually provide that help. The harmful-technical-knowledge dataset probes the first; the propensity dataset probes the second.

A model can have dangerous knowledge and still reliably refuse to share it. So knowledge alone doesn’t establish that its safeguards have failed. But if you can elicit harmful assistance despite those safeguards, that suggests the underlying capability remains accessible and the protections aren’t robust enough.

The important caveat is that these are evaluations under particular conditions. They don’t, by themselves, tell us how often someone would succeed in the real world or whether the assistance would enable a successful attack. I’d interpret the failures as evidence of gaps in the safeguards, rather than a complete measure of real-world risk.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes knowledge from willingness to provide help, but does not say the datasets differ by whether harmful intent is explicitly declared.

r002.rationale: It gives no compliance percentages or relationship between average compliance and compliance on explicitly malicious questions.

r003.rationale: It describes safeguard gaps and insufficient robustness, but does not attribute the failures to developers making insufficient effort.

r004.rationale: It does not explain why the harm domains were selected or mention expectations of stronger safeguards there.

r005.rationale: It makes no prediction about vulnerability outside the evaluated CBRN and explosives domains.
